title: Intel's Crescent Island AI Server GPU Gets a Name and Specs: Meet the Intel GPU D-Series
gist: At OCP Global Summit Intel named Crescent Island the Intel GPU D-Series and locked specs for the GPU D270: 1.3 PFLOPS FP8, 1.5TB/s LPDDR5X bandwidth, 350W air cooled, up to 480GB memory. It is about 40% below AMD's MI350P on FP8 but pitches efficiency and capacity; cards are sampling with no launch date, so a release looks like 2027.

insights.claim: Crescent Island is Intel's first commercial AI-focused data center GPU since Ponte Vecchio in 2021, following cancellation of Ponte successors Rialto Bridge in 2023 and Falcon Shores in 2025, and was announced as an interim cost- and power-optimized AI inference product.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Intel's repeated cancellations leave it a late, niche entrant in AI accelerators; execution risk remains.
insights.quote: With two of Ponte’s successors canceled over the last few years – Rialto Bridge in 2023 and then Falcon Shores in 2025

insights.claim: Crescent Island is not meant to match flagship chips like NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra or AMD's MI455X in performance, but will be a lot smaller and cheaper.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Intel is targeting the cost-sensitive inference tier rather than competing at the top end.
insights.quote: The resulting chip is not meant to be on the same performance level as flagship chips such as NVIDIA’s Blackwell Ultra or AMD’s MI455X

insights.claim: Crescent Island uses Xe3P, an enhanced Xe3 architecture with far more XMX matrix engines and a far larger LPDDR5X memory subsystem of up to 480GB, so Intel is banking on a massive matrix-math Xe3 with a large LPDDR5X pool to compete among inference accelerators.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Betting on cheap LPDDR5X capacity rather than HBM is a distinct cost and supply-chain angle versus rivals.
insights.quote: Intel is banking on a massive matrix math version of Xe3 that is backed by a large LPDDR5X memory pool of up to 480GB
insights.locator: Most recently, Intel delivered an update

insights.claim: The Intel GPU D270 has 32 Xe cores, 256 XMX engines at about 2.5GHz, 1.3 PFLOPS peak FP8 matrix and 10.2 TFLOPS FP64 vector throughput, 32MB L2, PCIe Gen5 x16, ECC and a 350W TDP in an air-cooled PCIe CEM form factor.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Concrete specs allow direct comparison against rival PCIe inference cards.

insights.claim: The D270 offers 1.5TB/s of memory bandwidth from a 20 chip, 80 channel LPDDR5X bus clocked around 9375MT/s.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: LPDDR5X bandwidth at 1.5TB/s is far below HBM-class parts, shaping which inference workloads suit it.
insights.quote: the flagship card will offer 1.5TB/second of memory bandwidth, which comes courtesy of its hefty 20 chip, 80 channel LPDDR5X memory bus

insights.claim: Intel's own card ships with 160GB of LPDDR5X (20x8GB chips) while ODM partners can offer up to 480GB using 24GB chips, a far larger capacity than any other PCIe accelerator announced thus far.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Memory capacity is Intel's clearest differentiator for large-model or long-context inference.
insights.quote: an extreme amount of memory enabled by 24GB LPDDR5X chips and a far larger capacity than any other PCIe form factor accelerator announced thus far
insights.locator: Finally, Intel has once again confirmed

insights.claim: The published figures are very close to industry expectations, so Crescent Island neither surpasses nor fails to meet expectations.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: No positive or negative surprise; the thesis now rests on pricing and real-world efficiency.
insights.quote: Crescent Island is not surpassing expectations, but it is not failing to meet them, either.
insights.locator: In practice, these figures are very close

insights.claim: AMD's PCIe CEM MI350P offers a theoretical 2.3 PFLOPS of dense FP8, so the 1.3 PFLOPS Crescent Island card is some 40% lower, though theoretical throughput alone rarely predicts real-world results.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A raw FP8 gap of roughly 40% means Intel must win on efficiency, prefill performance or price.
insights.quote: a Crescent Island card comes in some 40% lower
insights.locator: As to whether 1.3 PFLOPs of FP8

insights.claim: Power and cooling may be the bigger differentiator: the flagship Crescent Island card is a 350 Watt air-cooled part while MI350P's highest performance configuration is 600 Watts, and Intel is touting performance per watt over absolute speed.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Air-cooled 350W cards fit traditional servers without liquid cooling, widening the addressable base for inference.
insights.quote: The flagship Crescent Island card is a 350 Watt card that can be air cooled, whereas MI350P’s highest performance configuration is 600 Watts.
insights.locator: The bigger differentiator there will likely be power

insights.claim: Competitiveness will hinge on architectural efficiency versus AMD's CDNA 4, especially if Intel does meaningfully better in prefill, traditionally where GPU architectures bottleneck in data center-scale workloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Watch independent prefill benchmarks, which would be the key proof point for Intel's inference claim.
insights.quote: Especially if Intel can do meaningfully better in prefill

insights.claim: Crescent Island cards will be sold as the Intel GPU D-Series, with the GPU D270 as the first and only card so far, a double-wide PCIe card for traditional servers; Intel is dropping the Data Center GPU Max (and Flex) branding although the D-Series is effectively Max's successor.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A fresh brand signals a clean break from Ponte Vecchio-era GPU products.
insights.quote: the GPU D-series is its own product through and through
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Crescent Island cards are finally getting

insights.claim: Intel is sampling cards to customers but has not announced a launch date or confirmed a launch in 2026, so AI server vendors seeking PCIe inference alternatives should look to 2027, and price remains unannounced.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Late availability and unknown pricing delay any share impact from Intel; competitors keep a 2026 window.
insights.quote: Intel is confirming that they are sampling cards to customers.
insights.locator: Wrapping things up, with today’s announcement
